title: Carbon 13 [In progress]
summary:
Oil is many things. While oil in general consists predominantly of hydrocarbons, the length and structure of hydrocarbon molecules is variable, and the proportion of longer heavier molecules and the presence of other elements, including Oxygen and Sulphur, varies depending on the source (Bensaude-Vincent and Loeve 2024: 116). Oil can be easy to extract, concentrated in large fields close to the surface, or much less easily accessible, and extracted from the deep sea, and it can contain greater or lesser quantities of impurities. Through its exploration and extraction, oil’s existence is multiplied further. An oil reserve is not characterised only by its volume, or its chemical composition. Oil reserves do not have such well-defined dimensions. A reserve is a socio-material assemblage: a resource, which for a period, can be exploited, given prevailing technology and prices, and geopolitical circumstances (Richardson and Weszkalnys 2014). Moreover, the size of the reserve depends on estimations of what can be extracted, not on what exists independently of the process of exploration and extraction, and its geophysical and geochemical investigation (Bowker 1994). As prices rise, oil reserves necessarily increase as less accessible fields become potentially profitable to exploit. And when prices decline, some oil reserves will decrease in size, as they become commercially unviable. No wonder, given this variability, that what is often said to be the price of oil, as it is quoted in public news media, does not reflect the price of oil ‘in general’. Rather, it is the price of oil from a particular location, quoted on a particular exchange. In Western Europe, the most frequently quoted price of oil is Brent crude, or oil from the Brent oil field in the North Sea, and in the United States it is West Texas Intermediate (WTI), at a price quoted on the New York exchange.

If oil is often differentiated by a name that refers to both a price and a location, and by its molecular composition, it also varies geographically in more unexpected ways. In this chapter I turn to consider the remarkable significance of the ratio of two stable isotopes of Carbon, Carbon-12 and Carbon-13 in any sample of oil. Carbon-13 (or 13C) is much less common (typically 1%) than 12C (99%), but the ratio between 12C and 13C can nonetheless vary significantly. Why should the geography of isotopic composition matter, and how did it come to matter, given that both the commercial value and chemical properties of oil, in any of its many forms, does not depend on the relative abundance of the two isotopes?
analysis:
Here I make two arguments about the remarkable significance of 13C, the work that it does, its lives (Bensaude-Vincent and Loeve 2024). One is that an interest in the isotopic composition of oil, and the commercial value of knowledge of this composition, is an element of what I will call, borrowing the term from Stuart Hall, a conjuncture – an event that emerges from and generates relations between distinct historical movements. 13C both acquired and generated significance at the height of the cold war, forging a relation between the development of nuclear physics and nuclear weapons, on the one hand, and the mid-20th century expansion and dominance of the US oil industry, on the other. It is in this conjuncture, that the agency of 13C is made manifest. These were also circumstances in which the field of organic geochemistry developed in the early 1960s While Brent and West Texas were becoming markers for the global oil price, the isotopic composition of oil from another specific location, La Habra, Southern California, became the global standard against which the isotopic composition of oil came to be calibrated. As historians and sociologists of science have long argued, global standards and reference materials such as this, often have quite local and historical origins (Schaffer 1997, Lezaun 2012), and their existence has often been bound up with the development of political and commercial empires.

Secondly, I follow the history and geography of 13C as a ‘material abstraction’ (Bensaude-Vincent). As we shall see, 13C becomes an index of the way in which past environmental change affects the composition of oil in the present, pointing towards connections between the deep time of oil and its embeddedness in the global economy. 13C responds to variations in temperature and depth, distinguishing itself from 12C. Yet, at the same time, the changing ratio between C13 and C12 in the atmosphere came to indicate the contribution of oil production to the atmosphere’s ongoing transformation. In the nexus of relations between the cold war, mid-20th century capitalism and climate change, 13C turns out to be a surprisingly important intermediary; an interscalar vehicle that crosses the lines between inert and living matter, geos and bios, between the nuclear and oil industries and environmental research, forging connections between the subatomic with the geopolitical, and between human history and nonhuman time. In this chapter, I give a brief introduction to the concept of the isotope in chemical theory, and its material abstraction. I turn to consider the conjuncture of the late 1940s-early 60s which witnessed the translation of mass spectrometry from the Manhattan programme to geochemistry, the development of organic geochemistry, the movement of oil samples from Southern California to Vienna, and a remarkable debate about oil’s biogeochemical origins. In the final section I turn to consider how Carbon 13 acquired a new life as an indicator of environmental change in the present.
